new_content.text: The RNN experiments suggested that Luong Attention improved reply coherence and relevance, but contextual errors remained. We therefore investigated pretrained Transformer models for V5. Self-attention provides direct connections between tokens and permits greater parallelisation during training than recurrent processing [1]. Our aim was to generate a contextually appropriate reply in Standard English and a natural Singlish counterpart that preserved the same intended meaning. A stronger architecture was treated as a hypothesis to evaluate, rather than a guarantee of contextual understanding.

Development proceeded from mT5 adaptation and style conditioning to English-first rewriting, followed by experiments with larger language models. Throughout these experiments, contextual appropriateness, cross-style meaning preservation and natural Singlish were considered separately. This distinction was necessary because two replies could express the same incorrect answer, while a faithful copy of Standard English could still fail the requested local style.
3.3.1 Initial Training Plan

The main initial model was google/mt5-base, a multilingual encoder–decoder Transformer with approximately 582 million parameters in our implementation. Its multilingual text-to-text pretraining made it a suitable starting point for English-based conversations containing Singlish features [2]. The plan comprised two broad stages: full-model language and conversation adaptation, followed by adaptation to the project reply-generation task. The implementation further divided the first stage into span-corruption adaptation, recorded as Stage 0, and public-dialogue training, recorded as Stage 1. The project-specific phase was recorded as Stage 2 [P1].

During language adaptation, the model continued learning through span corruption on 96,295 text chunks from CoSEM and the NUS SMS Corpus. Fifteen per cent of tokens were masked in spans with a mean length of three tokens. The subsequent public-dialogue phase trained next-reply generation on 76,052 DailyDialog pairs and an 80,000-pair CoSEM sample. DailyDialog examples were assigned the STANDARD prefix and CoSEM examples the LOCAL prefix. These source-based labels supplied broad style supervision; they did not provide paired English and Singlish versions of the same reply.

Project-specific adaptation then used the 190 team-authored training conversations. Each supplied one Standard English target and one local target, giving 380 reply examples. Another 180 reply examples were extracted from the training histories, producing 560 supervised rows. Inputs included explicit Friend/You speaker labels to distinguish the person receiving a message from the person composing the reply. A single Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter learned both styles, with textual task prefixes selecting the requested output. LoRA freezes the adapted base weights and trains small additional matrices [3]. In this configuration, 1,769,472 parameters, approximately 0.30% of the base model size, were trainable.

new_content.text: FP32 was used after FP16 training produced non-finite losses in the project runs. Early comparisons also examined mT5-small, full-model task fine-tuning and LoRA. The settings above describe the historical mT5-base baseline; later experiments changed the learning rate, input budget or adaptation method and should not be treated as repetitions of an identical recipe.

The initial model could produce fluent short replies, but the independently generated English and Singlish versions frequently expressed different decisions or actions. Common problems included changing acceptance into refusal, confusing who should lend or borrow an item, and answering a different question from the one asked. Some local outputs remained Standard English, while others relied on repetitive or unsuitable local markers. An audit of 40 sampled CoSEM reply pairs also found 13 whose replies did not answer their associated messages, identifying noise in the adaptation data [P1]. This was a small data audit, rather than an estimate of error across the entire corpus.
3.3.2 Adaptations

The main change was to generate the reply in English first and then rewrite that exact draft into Singlish. Previously, both outputs were generated independently from the conversation. In the revised pipeline, the LOCAL_REWRITE input contained the conversation and the generated English reply. The same shared mT5 adapter performed both tasks. Training used reviewed English anchors; inference used the model’s own English draft. This gave both outputs a common intended response, while allowing the local version to change grammar and phrasing [P2].

The training targets were also aligned in a separate derivative of the 190-item corpus. Fourteen English targets were corrected, and Gemma4 12B supplied candidate local rewrites. An assistant reviewed the drafts and revised 117 local targets. These were generated and assistant-edited targets, rather than independently validated human labels. The original team-authored records were preserved. Three arms compared the original targets with independent generation, aligned targets with independent generation, and aligned targets with sequential rewriting. All used the same adapted base, rank-16 q/v LoRA, learning rate 3 × 10⁻⁴, batch size 16 and 784 optimizer updates. The source limit increased to 192 tokens, while the output limit remained 48 tokens.

On the same 50 validation conversations, the seed-425 aligned-target independent arm preserved meaning in 19 cases, compared with 17 for the original arm. Adding sequential rewriting increased this to 42 cases. The original and sequential arms were then reviewed across seeds 425, 1 and 2. Table 3.3b reports mean pass counts per 50 conversations; the additional seeds repeat the same conversations [P2].

new_content.text: English-first rewriting produced a repeated improvement in paired meaning and local style, but contextual appropriateness remained approximately unchanged. A correct rewrite could faithfully preserve an incorrect English answer. For example, the model could still ask an uninformed peer for printer instructions or reverse charger ownership. The next experiments therefore investigated the content generator as well as the style rewriter.

Several interventions gave narrow improvements without establishing a consistent overall upgrade. Table 3.3c groups the main experimental families; individual checkpoints and seeds are retained in the project records. The observations explain why these variants were not sufficient replacements for the stronger reference pipeline, rather than showing that the underlying methods cannot work.

Earlier checkpoints did not consistently improve English adequacy. In the matched 600-addition study, English passed 36/50 in both arms, while local adequacy fell from 38/50 to 25/50. More data alone was insufficient.

Full tuning fit a 24-example diagnostic more easily than LoRA. On scaled data, validation loss deteriorated after early epochs in some runs; lower selected loss still did not establish correct conversational replies.

Copying, clause loss, changed tense and polarity reversals remained. One full-context rewrite changed an available Friday into a refusal. A 30-case human comparison of an earlier hybrid recorded 19 both-bad judgments.
Reply-act conditioning and target repair
Supply acceptance/refusal/counterproposal information and audit target consistency

Some supplied acts affected the output, and photo-sending direction improved in a repair study. Correct supplied refusal acts could still produce acceptance of incompatible times or unaffordable meals. Other examples regressed.
Separate adapters, output heads and context objectives
Separate English/style learning, test linear/MLP output heads, and restore extra history supervision

No general quality improvement was established. Separate adapters increased copying in the tested recipe; output-head variants remained meaning-unstable. The two-seed history-objective study showed mixed loss changes and persistent role/time errors.
Auxiliary facts and answerability; explicit planning
Teach factual structure and generate context notes before replying
Auxiliary prediction and note generation could be learned, but facts or roles were sometimes wrong. Even correct diagnostic notes could be ignored by the reply decoder.
Reward-model and structured RL diagnostics
Check whether preference or reward signals could guide factual decisions
Reward audits made contextual mistakes, while a small structured RL/SFT comparison selected its unchanged starting checkpoint. These diagnostics did not establish improved free-form reply generation.

new_content.text: These findings suggested that surface fluency and task fitting were easier to obtain than reliable use of conversational constraints. However, the experiments changed different combinations of data, objectives, adapter coverage and training duration. They do not identify a single cause of mT5’s limitations. Token-level validation loss was useful for checkpoint selection within a fixed setup, but it was insufficient for deciding whether a reply was contextually correct. Raw losses were also unsuitable for ranking model families with different tokenizers.
3.3.3 Larger Models

We next explored AI Singapore’s SEA-LION-v1-3B, a decoder-only language model pretrained on languages used in Southeast Asia [4]. This provided a larger candidate with regional-language exposure. Early direct English/local training produced useful phrasing on some conversations, but the two styles could still disagree. We therefore applied the English-first pipeline to SEA-LION as well. Recorded examples showed improved preservation of some budget refusals, dietary decisions and return directions, alongside continuing errors in exact times, ownership and completion status [P9].

For the SEA-LION pipeline used in the shared comparison, public adaptation used 117,634 reply pairs: 53,691 CoSEM and 63,943 DailyDialog examples. The frozen backbone was adapted through rank-8 LoRA, with alpha 16 and dropout 0.05. Public training used one full pass at a learning rate of 5 × 10⁻⁵ and an effective batch size of 16. Project tuning then used 790 conversations, comprising the original 190 and 600 corrected generated additions, with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and an effective batch size of eight. The English checkpoint was selected at epoch two. An anchored rewrite stage used 745 eligible pairs at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁵; its selected epoch-one adapter was followed by a contrastive repair branch, which retained the original English checkpoint and selected local repair step 25. These settings correspond to the SEA-LION pipeline summarized in Section 3.5.

new_content.caption: Table 3.3d. Further SEA-LION experiments and the limits of their improvements [P12].
rows: Direct dual-style replies versus English-first rewriting
English-first rewriting repaired several acceptance/refusal and ownership mismatches. Exact numbers, return direction and faithful preservation of the English draft remained difficult.
Greedy decoding, beam search and repetition controls

Beam search improved some wording and individual decisions, but did not consistently fix contextual constraints. Plain beam-4/8 decoding also produced repetition or output-length-limit failures in some cases.
Contrastive factual repair
Training increased the likelihood or ranking of selected correct synthetic replies, but these teacher-forced diagnostics did not demonstrate a general improvement in generated conversations.
Copy suppression and local-target wording changes

Some variants reduced identical English/local strings or improved isolated phrasing. Reduced copying could coexist with reversed ownership or added timing claims, so copying was not used as a quality metric.
Latest-turn/layout repair and context policies
The neural repair arms did not establish a consistent gain. Optional deterministic context policies had limited rule coverage and were assessed separately from standalone model capability.
Answerability/abstention training

The corrected variant improved abstention on constructed missing-fact questions, but that narrower goal did not match a reply coach that should offer plausible, useful drafts. It did not establish overall conversational improvement.
Single versus multiple valid continuations

Multiple-reference and contrastive variants produced some more useful continuations, but the recorded review remained mixed. Better validation likelihood did not by itself establish contextual reliability.
Audited data, learning rates and warmup/decay
Later B/C pipelines tested revised data and schedules. Several factors changed together, so any difference could not be attributed to the scheduler alone.

new_content.text: Later exploratory runs used an audited subset of 768 conversations and 766 eligible rewrite pairs. The SEA-LION C recipe used English/rewrite peak learning rates of 5 × 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁵ respectively, eight epochs per stage, and 5% linear warmup followed by cosine decay. Qwen2.5-3B was investigated as a similarly sized multilingual causal language model with approximately 3.09 billion parameters (Qwen Team, n.d.). An initial fresh-adapter comparison trained SEA-LION and Qwen for four epochs per task without project public adaptation. A subsequent Qwen run reproduced the full 117,634-example public pass and the audited C task/rewrite recipe, selecting epoch two for both English generation and rewriting. These were later research comparisons; they did not replace the SEA-LION repair-step-25 pipeline used in the shared system evaluation.

A separate retrospective development study compared saved outputs on all 50 original validation conversations. The mT5 reference was the historical shared-intent seed-1 checkpoint at update 784; the larger-model references were the later audited SEA-LION C pipeline and the full-public-recipe Qwen pipeline. Their incoming messages, histories and speaker labels were verified to match. The mT5 reference used the reviewed 190-conversation task dataset, whereas the later larger-model pipelines used the audited expanded dataset. This compares complete trained systems rather than isolating model size or architecture, and it is separate from the 60-conversation evaluation of the final systems in Section 4.

One assistant reviewed each English/local pair using four criteria: English contextual adequacy, local contextual adequacy, meaning preservation, and natural recognizable Singlish. Plausible new personal choices were allowed because the outputs are selectable drafts; explicit contradictions, reversed roles and missed requests were treated as errors. Uncertain judgments were recorded separately and did not count as passes. The review was non-blind, and all inputs had already been used extensively in development. The counts below are exploratory review outcomes, not independent human accuracy or final-test results.

new_content.text: Both replies were judged contextually adequate in 28 mT5 cases, 41 SEA-LION cases and 42 Qwen cases. The larger-model pipelines therefore appeared stronger on contextual response generation in this review. Qwen gave the highest English adequacy count, but its local output more often remained neutral Standard English. SEA-LION achieved the highest combined count, 30/50 compared with 27/50 for Qwen and 23/50 for mT5. The difference between the two larger models was small, and no statistical superiority or generalisation claim is made. The historical three-criterion mT5 study and this four-criterion review used different review definitions and must be interpreted separately.

The case-level results illustrate the trade-off. For ITEM-B-057, the peer asks to borrow the user’s charger. mT5 replied “Sure, I’ll borrow it,” reversing the roles, while SEA-LION and Qwen correctly offered the charger. However, SEA-LION reversed the update direction in ITEM-B-034 by asking the absent peer to explain what they missed; Qwen correctly offered a class summary. Qwen also introduced errors during rewriting: in ITEM-D-038, an English promise to wait for the peer became “wait for me” in the local version. These examples show why fluent English and faithful local rewriting require separate assessment.

The Qwen experiments also prompted a closer examination of whether this dataset strongly tested regional-language understanding. The incoming-message annotations show that 112/190 training messages and 30/50 validation messages list local terms. Singlish is tagged in 113/190 training messages and 31/50 validation messages. Pinyin or Chinese is tagged in only 11/190 training messages and 2/50 validation messages. These are counts of the existing annotations, whose coverage is imperfect, rather than a complete linguistic analysis [P11].

A manual assistant audit of the 50 incoming validation messages classified eight as containing regional lexical content, such as kiasu, dabao, chiong or na li. Fifteen primarily contained regional pragmatic markers, apologies or greetings; eight primarily used colloquial syntax; and nineteen were general English or texting. This classification describes the incoming message only; histories and generated replies can contain additional local features. It separates content vocabulary from particles and grammar for analysis, without implying that the latter require no local competence.

This audit supports a narrower conclusion than claiming regional-language understanding was unimportant. Most validation conversations were short, English-based exchanges with light local features. They placed substantial demands on general conversational skills such as tracking participants, timing and intent, but provided limited coverage of extended regional-language code-switching. Regional interpretation still mattered: Qwen treated na li as the place name “Na Li,” and all three systems failed to answer the underlying meeting-location question in ITEM-E-007. A dedicated regional-language benchmark would be needed to isolate that capability.

The development studies supported choosing SEA-LION as the V5 generator because it offered a useful balance of coherent replies and recognizable Singlish. Qwen remained a strong exploratory alternative for English content, while mT5 provided a smaller reference whose cross-style consistency improved with English-first rewriting. The later SEA-LION C/Qwen review does not establish a definitive ranking between those two research variants. The final system comparison and the decision to use SEA-LION directly for Standard English, with a separate local-wording refinement stage, are reported in Sections 3.4 and 4.
